missing.why: The two-call path is reachable in code, but the evidence record identifies unresolved policy treatment of malicious providers and notes that the borrower is trusted and can already block deposits.

missing.why: The demonstrated deposit lockout is also achievable through blockFromDeposits or revokeRole, so the evidence does not establish additional impact from this bypass.
missing.resolves_when: Demonstrate a concrete harm caused by the bypass that those existing powers cannot cause, with a supported scenario and affected party.

reason: The source supports the two-call bypass, but policy compliance for the actor and distinct impact remain unresolved. The supplied test output is contradictory, though clean reproduction would only strengthen the source-supported path.

evidence.claim: A role provider can bypass the documented grantRole restriction (cannot lower another provider's credential expiry) by first granting a later expiry to become lastProvider, then lowering the expiry; the report's own PoC shows the resulting effect (deposit lockout) is already achievable by the borrower via blockFromDeposits and by a lastProvider via revokeRole.
evidence.support_reason: In _grantRole (FixedTermLoanHooks.sol:441-470), the guard at line 426 allows replacement when status.lastProvider == msg.sender OR newExpiry > oldExpiry. A provider B can first call grantRole with a later expiry (passes newExpiry > oldExpiry, sets lastProvider=B at line 469/792), then call again with a lower expiry (passes status.lastProvider == msg.sender). The two-step bypass is reachable. Same logic in AccessControlHooks.sol:426.
preconditions: Borrower has added at least two role providers (A and B) with B's TTL > A's TTL
Provider B acts maliciously (or is compromised)
Victim has not yet deposited (known lenders retain withdrawal access)

missing_evidence.item: Policy determination on whether a malicious/compromised borrower-appointed role provider is an allowed actor for this finding
missing_evidence.why: The attack requires a role provider (appointed by the borrower) to act maliciously. The policy lists Borrowers as trusted and describes providers as borrower-controlled; the report itself concedes the borrower can already achieve the same lockout via blockFromDeposits and a lastProvider can revokeRole outright. Without a policy basis treating a malicious provider as in-scope, the path is not reachable under allowed actors.
missing_evidence.resolves_when: The contest policy explicitly states that malicious or compromised role providers are in-scope actors, or the judge rules that borrower-appointed providers are not trusted.

missing_evidence.item: Demonstration of an impact beyond what the borrower or a lastProvider can already do
missing_evidence.why: The report's own PoC shows the borrower can lock the victim out with blockFromDeposits and a lastProvider can revokeRole. The only novel effect is the two-call sequence, which does not produce a capability the trusted parties lack. Without a distinct impact, the severity claim is unsupported.
missing_evidence.resolves_when: A concrete scenario is shown where the two-call bypass causes harm that blockFromDeposits and revokeRole cannot, e.g. affecting a lender who is a known lender or affecting withdrawal access.

missing_evidence.item: Confirmation that the PoC compiles and runs against the audited commit
missing_evidence.why: The pasted forge output contains a compilation error (`unresolved symbol locals` in SphereXProtectedRegisteredBase.sol) yet reports PASS, which is internally contradictory. However, the code path is verifiable by reading _grantRole, so the claim does not depend on the test executing.
missing_evidence.resolves_when: A clean forge run without the compilation error is provided.
